title: Music for Remembering
sub: Grades 5–8 · Music · Marches, a Largo and the silence
objective: Students will listen to the music the exhibition plays in its two poster rooms and describe it by **tempo**, **dynamics** and **mood**. They will compare Sousa’s march *The Stars and Stripes Forever* with his funeral march *In Memoriam*, hear two pieces called **Largo**, by Dvořák and Handel, and think about bells and **silence** as sound. Then they will plan two minutes of remembrance in sound.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Music tells us how to feel before anyone speaks. The exhibition chose its music, its bells and its silence with care, and listening closely shows us how.

materials: Speakers, and the four recordings on the classroom screen
The listening guide on page 3, projected or printed
*The Memorial* open on a screen, for the two minutes’ silence
connection: **Online,** open each poster and listen to its room’s music as you read; play *When the Guns Fell Silent*; and keep the two minutes’ silence in *The Memorial*. **In the exhibition,** listen at the iPad Armistice audio station beside the display case.

steps.title: Music A, Music B
script: Play about thirty seconds of each, without saying what they are. *“Two rooms, two kinds of music. Which would you march to, and which would make you stand still?”* Take words for each: fast, proud, bright; slow, quiet, sad. Then: *“The Mini Museum plays one of these in a room about the young soldiers, and the other in a room about the moment the war ended. Which is which, and why?”*

screen.question: Two rooms, two kinds of music. Which would you march to, and which would make you stand still?

steps.purpose: Hear two kinds of music before naming them.
students: What words describe Music A? Music B?
Which would you put in a room about the end of a war?

steps.title: Two marches by Sousa
script: **Two marches (page 3).** The Doughboys room plays two marches by John Philip Sousa, one after the other: *The Stars and Stripes Forever* (1896), then *In Memoriam* (1881), his funeral march for President Garfield. Play a little of each. Students compare tempo, dynamics and mood. It is the same composer and the same kind of music, a march; what changes is its purpose, from marching in step to mourning.

clips.label: The Doughboys room
clips.sub: Sousa: “The Stars and Stripes Forever” (1896), then “In Memoriam” (1881)

screen.question: Same composer, same kind of music. What changes when a march becomes a funeral march?

steps.purpose: Compare a march and a funeral march by tempo, dynamics and mood.
students: Why might the room play both, one after the other?

steps.title: Two pieces called Largo
script: **Two pieces called Largo.** The When the Guns Fell Silent room plays the Largo from Dvořák’s Symphony no. 9, *From the New World*, on a record made by the Victor Concert Orchestra in 1912, then Handel’s *Largo*, from *Xerxes*, played on the cello by Victor Sorlin on a record made in 1908. *Largo* means very slow. Point out the surface sound of the old records, which the exhibition kept.

clips.label: The When the Guns Fell Silent room
clips.sub: Dvořák: Largo, from the “New World” Symphony; then Handel: “Largo,” on the cello

screen.question: Both are called Largo. What do they share?

steps.purpose: Hear a very slow tempo, and why it suits remembering.
students: What do you notice about the old records’ sound?
Why play slow music for the end of a war?

steps.title: Bells, wind and a bird
script: **Bells and silence.** As the poster reaches 11:00, bells strike. In the exhibition’s short film, the guns are cut dead at 11:00 and only the wind and a single bird remain. In 1919, Americans paused for two minutes at 11:00; Canada, Britain and France still keep the two-minute silence.

clips.label: The wind across the field
clips.sub: All that is left in the film after 11:00

clips.label: A single bird
clips.sub: The end of the film, after the guns have stopped

screen.question: After the guns stop, what is left to hear?

steps.purpose: Hear bells and near-silence as part of remembering.
students: Why might the film keep only wind and a single bird?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Play the recordings again as students work. All three levels use the same pieces.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Fill in a listening chart for the four pieces: fast or slow, loud or soft, and a mood word. Choose the piece that best fits remembering, and say why.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Compare Sousa’s march and his funeral march in a table. Explain why the room plays them one after the other, and what the Largo adds in the next room.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Plan two minutes of remembrance in sound for 11:00 on November 11, in four thirty-second parts, using music, bells, natural sound or silence, and justify each choice.

steps.purpose: Listen closely and plan in sound, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three use the same four pieces, the bells and the silence.

steps.title: Two minutes’ silence
script: Open *The Memorial*, choose *The silence at 11:00* and press *Keep two minutes’ silence now*. Afterward, ask: *what did you hear?* (The room, breathing, outside.) *Why might silence be the right sound for remembering?*

screen.text:
At 11:00 on November 11,
people pause in silence to remember.

steps.purpose: Keep the silence together, and listen to it.
students: What did you hear in the silence?
How was it different from the music?

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down; for the last, ask a Red Level composer to explain one choice in their plan.
steps.purpose: Check what each student can now do against the objectives.
